utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the witness is being brought in, I would just like to indicate I would like to save five minutes at the end of the day, perhaps, to raise a procedural scheduling matter. But I don't want to interrupt the witness's presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic. I'll have to return with you to some things we discussed on Friday because not everything was recorded correctly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document P1442.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you may remember that I showed you a log-book of events of the 15th of May, 1992. You're about to see it. And we commented on it on page 11644, line -- lines 5 through 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 955, which, in the meantime, was marked P1442.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This usually happens on Monday mornings. Just a bit of patience, please, Mr. Kezunovic. Mr. Kezunovic, you remember that we were reading this document. I showed it to you. It's dated the 15th of May, 1992, especially the last sentence where it says: "The daily reports were not submitted by CSB Doboj and CSB Trebinje." And then I put it to you that they didn't submit their reports because there were no communication lines with the com centre of the MUP headquarters. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that detail, but I don't see that in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence, sir, reads: "In the area of CSB Trebinje, there were no events interesting from the security point of view, and the daily reports were not submitted by the CSBs of Doboj and Trebinje." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the communication lines didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next intervention is about page -- page 11652, lines 18 and 19. You remember that I asked you the death of two of your staff who were ambushed in the surroundings of Caparde; they had, in the meantime, been transferred to national security. And we were able to remember the family name of one of them; his last name is Trobok [phoen]. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Trobok. His first name is Momir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to pages 11657. This is about document P1426.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you may remember that I showed you the document that will appear in a moment. It's an activity report of the Communications Department of Doboj CSB. It refers to the period from the 30th of July to the 30th of September, 1992, and it's dated 1 October 1992. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I quoted that document to you - and I'm referring to the third paragraph, the second sentence there. I'll paraphrase: Connection with the ministry has been set up by KT connections. The transcript of Friday reads KT or cryptographic connection. But KT stands for short-wave communication, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic. Mr. -- where are we in the English translation? The second sentence of the third paragraph reads that telephone and telefax communications with all of the above organs were established through the PTT. Is that the same sentence that are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, this -- it's the first -- it's the first sentence of the third paragraph. It starts with: "The telephone and telegraph communications with the Banja Luka CSB and a short-wave communication with ministry has been set up through the use of appropriate documents and devices."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the problem was that it was recorded in the transcript of 11th of June as KT or encrypted, so short wave or encrypted. And that's what I wanted to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, for these clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now please be shown P625.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an activity report of the MUP for April through December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page in the Serbian version is 36. It's marked FI20-1311. That's the ERN number. Could we please also see the corresponding English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, that we read the first paragraph where it says that the communications and cryptographic protection department of the ministry was one of those who, at the beginning, had the most problems. And then you explained what the word "problem" meant to you and that you considered it to be something that could not be solved. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this page, it says that in the headquarters of the Serbian ministry there was no technical equipment, no staff, and no -- and no other equipment necessary for work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the next page, in English, it says that the former MUP system had fallen apart and that there had also been deliberate severing of connections. It's the third paragraph from above, under item 3, the last sentence and the one before.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the next paragraph in the last sentence says: "... with the disintegration of the single teleprinter link, the system of cryptographic data protection for written communications in the organs ..." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. And it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the next paragraph says that in the newly established public security stations there is a lack of short-wave radio sets. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you remember that the information put forward in this report is correct as you put it forward in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this information is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the following page, page 37 in the Serbian, to the witness. I believe that the English page is the one we see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph says: "The problems with the UHF network were the lack of radio sets and difficulties with the work of the repeaters because the system is such that it can be used by anyone who has radio sets with the appropriate frequencies. And, among others, that there was also electronic jamming in the system ..." As far as can I tell, it's the third paragraph in the English text. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say here that the communications system in paragraph 3 -- and in English it's the sixth paragraph, it reads: "A particular problem for the communications system was the moving of the MUP from Vrace to Lukavica ..." as you said," and then to Pale and then to Bijeljina." Do you remember that also? And that is really true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and that is correct. It was a problem because we were constantly moving to a new location where there was nothing, not even a room for the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph, which is the fourth and I believe it's the seventh in English, you say -- you say that: Lately, which probably means late 1992, telex connections have been introduced in our -- telexes were installed in the MUP and the CSBs, and it -- have been installed in normal conditions ... amounts to almost 70 per cent installed connections. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this was written in early 1993, this report; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, even in early 1993, you don't have telex communications with about 30 per cent of the organisational units of the ministry; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because we can read here: The installment -- or, rather, the installing has begun recently. So actually these devices were connected in the latter half of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A significant share. But let me explain. In all the bodies which didn't have to move out from the facilities in which they were before the war, those facilities were completely equipped with telexes and everything else, but that doesn't mean that this equipment was functional. This connecting meant that both new equipment was procured and put into function or, alternatively, that old equipment was also made functional. And that is the explanation for the difference in numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this -- these telex connections, about which we can read in this paragraph, is the key segment of communications in the MUP because that's the way of sending out dispatches; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you will remember that in this document - and we commented on it on Friday, on page 11673, line 10 - we summarised that, according to the annual report, a total of 8.570 outgoing and incoming dispatches had gone through the telecoms or communications centre of the MUP headquarters. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that relates to the period from the 1st of April through the 31st of December?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, for 14 years you worked in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the administration for communications and cryptographic protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH had ten CSBs in its structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, the total annual amount of communications of the headquarters of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH, and I mean the system of dispatches, was several hundred thousand; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you mentioned an approximate number of 300.000 received and sent dispatches from the communications centre of the MUP HQ of the Socialist Republic of BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, if my math is correct, that means about 22.000 outgoing and incoming dispatches per month, on average?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we divide 300 through 12, that would be 20-odd thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are the data that are personally known to you because you were this number-two man in the administration for communications and cryptographic protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And certainly in the annual reports of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH this data can also be found.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And there were separate reports for cryptographic protection with regard to the number of encrypted dispatches for planning, for making code-books, et cetera, et cetera, because it was a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this data certainly refers to peacetime; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is logical to expect, isn't it, that at a time of imminent threat of war or in war time the number of dispatches rises significantly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's a logical assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with my assumption that in war time it would be logical to expect a rise of the number of dispatches by at least 30 per cent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. At least 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH had five CSBs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, by analogy, that's half the number as compared to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH, which means that it could be expected that the MUP of the RS had about 150.000 outgoing and incoming telegrams in peacetime; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is something in excess of 11.000 a month?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's a fact, isn't it, that, as we saw in the report, the total number of dispatches in nine months was 8.570, which is below the average monthly number of dispatches to be expected; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that this is the perfect illustration of the conditions -- of the condition of the system of communications of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to begin his cross-examination, I note without further comment that your very last question of the witness was to invite him to give a conclusion. Mr. Hannis didn't object. I suppose, again, the -- it was obvious, but no matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's -- I understand why you asked the question, but I'm just underlining the fact that at the end of the day it's a conclusion that you're inviting the witness to -- the witness to draw. And I underline witness as distinct from the Chamber. But, as I said, no matter; we understand why would you have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and I will be examining you on behalf of the Zupljanin Defence. While giving answers in your examination-in-chief, you spoke about being present at the meeting on the 11th of July in Belgrade. It was a meeting of the senior officials of MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please come closer to the microphone; interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now show you a summary of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters ask you to speak a little bit more into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to bend down since the microphone won't go up. Could we now see P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were already put questions by the Prosecutor regarding this document, and I will now show you the part that you did not discuss with the Prosecutor. And this is page 0324-1855. You remember that Mr. Zupljanin was at that meeting and he discussed certain matters; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that's page 8, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the bottom, the last paragraph of what Mr. Zupljanin said, where he says: "The functional system of communications has been broken down. Some talks were made concerning purchase of equipment with the representatives of the Rudi Cajavec company." This statement by Mr. Zupljanin at the meeting faithfully reflects the situation as it existed, not only in the territory of the Banja Luka CSB but almost in the entire RS territory.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was actually worse than depicted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also must know that after the conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least when it comes to Banja Luka CSB, that a large number of SJBs were attached to that CSB even though previously they were not covered by the Banja Luka CSB communications system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation changed significantly in relation to the situation before the war. There was an increase of 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because some 14 or 15 SJBs covered by the centre were under the centre before the war, and then once the conflict broke out, that number increased to 25 or 26 SJBs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, when it comes to a communications system, when CSBs sent their periodical reports, be it annual or reports compiled up to six months, they would always contain a chapter on encryption; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you a report of the Banja Luka centre from the 1st of January until the 30th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now please see Exhibit P595.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: See, this is a report that the centre provided on its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 18 in the Serbo-Croatian version; whereas in English it's page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see here the part dealing with other duties and tasks, and then underneath it, it says: "The functioning of the communications system and cryptographic protection." And then they go on to provide certain information about how the communications system functioned. And then they say - I'm paraphrasing - that the activities in the communications system and cryptographic protection were mostly centred on monitoring and repairing the communications system of the Banja Luka CSB. So that was their main job, the main job of signalsman in the centre, because there were frequent breakdowns, and they say that they had to repair the lines and establish communications where there had been none. And they mention Gornji Vakuf and -- and Bosanska Krupa. And then they mention that there was a breakdown in telephone communications; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I said telephone and telex communication lines.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Telephone and telex lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then they go on to say that due to war there were frequent breakdowns and disruptions in the lines. And then they mention the SJBs. And then they say that there were numerous breakdowns which were repaired as possible, as they could. And then they go on to say that all of this resulted in chaos in the communications system, especially in the telephone -- telegraphic communications. That is a accurate description of the system at the time in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then they go on to give an overview of telegrams, dispatches, that were received from January to June. And then they say that they received 9.956 open telegrams, 9.686 open telegrams which were transmitted. And then they have other figures. And since this is a report on the work of the entire centre, this report includes all SJBs and the CSB; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if we were to deduct some four months of normal work, January, February, March, and the larger part of April, then we get to a very significant fact. And this figure needs to be analysed in this context, that 60 to 70 per cent of the figures in this report pertain to peacetime; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bit more than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you another document, and that is P621. This is a report of the work of the CSB from the 1st of July to the 30th of September when there were war activities in the territory of the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now see, in Serbian, page 31, and the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the first paragraph. So in the territory of that CSB, they received 1.996 non-coded dispatches and 152 coded dispatches, and 1.385 non-coded and 43 coded were transmitted. So this figure applies to all SJBs and the centre for the period of three months, which is a very small figure as compared to regular communication; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And if I may add something; it's an explanation: The public is not informed of this. Only people who are professionally involved in this know about it. In peacetime, all members of the service sit in their offices, except for operatives who are on the ground, the uniformed policemen who have ultra short radios. There are no disruptions, no interceptions, everything is functioning routinely, and they can do their work calmly without any problems and hindrances in communications. During war time, you have to understand that it is not two offices fighting. It's a war that takes place on the ground. And people face two problems. There was a lack of communication between -- between communications centres and then there was a shortage of operatives and personnel on the ground who were supposed to stay in touch with the communications centre. They were supposed to provide information to the MUP seat based on which reports and dispatches were drafted and then forwarded elsewhere. So we have a complete disruption, breakdown in communications from the source of events to the seats of organisational units. And then there was another problem in communications between different communications centres that was supposed to stay in touch. This is why this problem is so complex. If we were to look at it from a simplistic point of view, just on the basis of these reports, then somebody could perhaps draw a conclusion that we were not professionally capable as a service; but as I have said to you previously, this was one of the major problems that simply could not be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to these reports of lower organisational units, especially SJBs and CSBs, a dispatch that was sent to SJBs would be treated as a sent dispatch; and then SJBs, once they received it, they record it as a received dispatch; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Whereas, in fact, it's the same dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at it that way. But the communications centres have different records as to what they received and what they sent. And it's true for all communications centres. So there is some overlapping; you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the figure should actually be lower. We should have this in mind. We should half these numbers, right, we should divide them by two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's, in principle right, but not -- not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could the witness be shown 2D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the work of the CSB for the first nine months of 1991. At that time, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now see page 14 in the Serbian, which is page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you were at the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you please look at page 4 -- paragraph 4 from the top where it says that in the telex -- in the teleprinter system, a total of 188.168 telegrams were received both uncoded and coded, and 39.858 were handed in, which is some over 200.000 dispatches, just for the first nine months of 1991. So if you compare these numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I pose a question or an interjection, Your Honour. On the document, I read -- says "telegrams." The question now is about dispatches. Can I have it clarified with the witness whether all dispatches are telegrams and whether all telegrams are dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there was a mistake in interpretation. It says here in the teleprinter system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "In the teleprinter system, a total of 188.168 telegrams were received." My question is: Are all telegrams dispatches; are all dispatches telegrams? Because the second question that was asked by my learned friend said "dispatches." And it's not clear from this document whether all telegrams are dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the problem obviously is with the translation. The Serbian text - and this can be probably proved by if the interpreters would be kind to read this. The original says: In the teleprinter system, a total 188.168 "depesa" was received. And sent: 39.858 "depesa." So it doesn't -- it refers to the very same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To -- to -- in order to clarify this, which is, as Mr. Zecevic has pointed out, may be a matter of translation, and even in English the terms tend to be interchangeable in popular usage, although technically there is probably a distinction. Perhaps a way out of this is for Mr. Krgovic to inquire of the witness what his understanding was and then build from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, we had a minor problem with interpretation. How do you understand this "depesa"? So these are not telegrams; these are "depesas"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is "depesa," a dispatch. We never used the word "telegram" in our service. It's the same thing. Dispatches in our internal system were used under that name. A dispatch is nothing else but a telegram. Except that the text that I have here says "in the teleprinter system." So there should be no dilemmas as to what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That is, dispatches are sent via the teleprinter system; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And let me return to my initial question: If you compare this number of dispatches from the peacetime period of the first nine months in 1991 and compare them with the data from 1992 that I showed you, that isn't even 10 per cent of the total amount of communications; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, I want to follow up with one of those last questions. In your answer, you said "everything is a dispatch." I'm confused because I understood in some of your testimony in direct that not every message that was sent by the teleprinter system or by fax in the RS MUP was what you considered to be a dispatch. I had understood from your -- from your earlier testimony that, for you, a dispatch, the meaning had a connection with the content and with the volume of the communication. Am I misunderstanding? Did you not say before the dispatch was something that was usually brief and it required some urgency? It was a request for information or it was a direction to carry out some kind of action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your dilemma. I tried to explain that to you. Anything received in the communications centre to be sent out in any form is treated as a dispatch. During the proofing we spoke about it, and there was the comment that everything that was not urgent or of an operative nature was sent out that way, and it is included in the total number of communications. They would not have been treated as dispatches if they had been transmitted by couriers. So, in peacetime, everything that wasn't urgent was sent by regular mail, which certainly transmitted a high -- larger number of documents than were transmitted by technical means, electronic means. So anything that wasn't urgent or of an operative nature was part of the total number of documents that were treated as dispatches. And certainly these numbers show the total amount of everything that was transmitted through the communications system. So the number of dispatches from the operative point of view is smaller than the number that we'll find in these statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me follow up on that. You said "everything that was transmitted through the communications system." I infer from that that there were some things that were transmitted through some system other than your communications centre. Is -- would that -- would I be correct in inferring that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is possible, but this is not the only possibility. Possibly the original document that was drawn up by some organisational unit was submitted to be transmitted through the electronics communications system. And if it had to be encrypted, then that would be done, but it would be entered as a dispatch to account for the use of resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If there were some other administration within the MUP headquarters that sent a communication not through your centre, for example, state security or national security, as it was later called, did they have separate communication facilities available to them outside your centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about the minister's office, Minister Stanisic. At any time during 1992, did his office have any kind of communication equipment that they could use to send a message without sending it through your centre? For example, a fax machine?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible they had one, but that was not my responsibility. My responsibility was to establish a communications centre and draw up instructions for the work of that centre, for the staff working there, as well as instructions for the work and conduct of all ministry staff. Everybody was duty-bound to read those instructions because they had to know what they are allowed and what they're not allowed to do and what they can transmit. So if anybody was in breach of these rules and I found out, I would intervene to prevent them from repeating that. Of course, if I didn't know, I couldn't intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I understood from your earlier testimony that in the early weeks of -- of the war - April and May - you were in Vrace -- physically located in Vrace and Lukavica for part of the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at least for a part of that time the minister was physically located in Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the minister in Pale was using to send and receive communications during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that already. I established two communications centre in parallel. They both belonged to the MUP HQ organisationally. That's the communications centre at Pale and the communications centre at Vrace. When you hear those designations "communications centre," you understand them to be units that are fully equipped with technical means, staff, and everything else. But both communications centres were in the same situation. They were both established from scratch. We first provided a number of telephone lines at Vrace, but then they were disconnected. And then we took those two numbers -- the two lines from the two neighbouring houses and then we were somehow able to supply one fax machine for each for -- to be able to transmit some messages. But in the early days, our capacities were very modest, both in terms of equipment and staff. So, in normal conditions we couldn't even provide round-the-clock operational capabilities. The staff would sleep at their workplaces, and if in case of need they would be awoken to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt, but the 21 -- page 21, 24, I believe the witness explained what kind of messages were sent by fax. Maybe you can clarify that. It says here, "some messages," but that's not what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, you heard what Mr. Zecevic said. Can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain to me what this is about because I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I do either, but he said in your last answer you mention that: "... we were somehow able to supply one fax machine for each for -- to be able to transmit some messages. But in the early days, our capacities were very modest ..." Mr. Zecevic thought you said something different. Rather than to be able to transmit "some messages," you said something different. Transmit a certain kind of message? Unfortunately, I don't know Serbian, and I can't tell what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that -- if this is what the question was about, to explain what kind of messages. If there was a fax machine at the communications centre, then we could only send out open messages and only to those to who we were physically capable of transmitting it. These are the messages I meant. Not all messages, certainly, for this reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in 1992, did some RS MUP personnel use the fax machines to send out messages that should have been coded and not sent on fax? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this wasn't supposed to happen. Of course, I wasn't on duty all the time to watch them, but the signalsmen were not supposed to do that. That wasn't allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you can't rule out the possibility that that didn't happen because you weren't able to watch every fax machine in the RS MUP 24 hours a day; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't supposed to watch any one fax machine. Only if I happened to be there and talk to them and watch what they were doing, learn about their problems. Only then would I be in the position to learn something or hearing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a couple of questions to try and clarify for me something about the number of dispatches sent in -- in 1992 and how those were kept track of in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we look first at Exhibit 1D73. This was tab 20 in my original package.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, we've looked at this one before. And you'll see that the number of this document at the top is 01-25 from -- from the minister, and it has to do with the CSB heads appointing personnel to certain positions within the CSBs. Now, keep in mind that number, 01-25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look now at Exhibit P1428. And I need to look at page 3 of the English, and it's also page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I want to look at item number 9. And if I could have the left half of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we discussed this earlier in your testimony I think you had agreed with me that the entry in sent and received dispatches under number 9 apparently refers to that document we just looked at, Exhibit 1D73, and it's the Serb MUP number 01-25. And my question is: As I understood explanations we've had about how documents were numbered, it appears that before 25 April 1992 there must have been a series of documents that were 01-1 through 01-24, some 24 other documents from the minister, but we're only at number 9 of dispatches sent. What does that say about those other documents? Were they sent by some other means and not recorded in here? Can you help with us an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these are two totally different numbers. What I can see on the screen now, at item 9, reads "Serb MUP number 01-" and then there's nothing. You can see -- can you see? And below that, there's the date, 25 April 1992 -- or, rather, 25/04. So there is no number; it just reads "01-" and there's an empty space after that. And below that the date is 25/04/92. And the previous document that you have just shown, as far as I remember, is, indeed, marked 01-25. Whether there is really a coincidence that the previous document had -- was numbered 25 as the 25th document in a sequence drafted in the office, that is a coincidence between that serial number and the date, the 25th, is a conclusion I cannot make. But here, the number is missing. It only reads "01-" and then no number after that. Then what we see on the screen now is a document of the communications centre. And the previous one is a document from the organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point, but you'll see under the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Is a list of documents from the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I take your point. But from our prior discussion in your direct testimony, we showed you that document. And you'll see here in the list, under summary of the content, that this document in item number 9 is described as decision on powers of heads of security centres. From having just looked at that document a few minutes ago. Or do I need to go back and show you the contents? That's what this was about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the title of the document as entered here, then it's the same document. If not, then they are -- then we're talking about different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 13 is described as MUP and BiH 01-26, dated the next day, the 26th of April, 1992, and is described as a supplemental memo regarding reception of workers with attachments. Keep that number in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit P1420.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, it's not the best copy, but at the top you can see this is number 01-26, and it is addressed to the five heads of the CSBs. And the first line under the addressees -- you say -- you can see it says: "In accordance with our act number 01-18/92 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go back to the log of dispatches, P1428, to page 4 of the English and B/C/S once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You see item 13, 01-26, 26 April, and makes reference to memo 01-18/92. Would you agree with me that the document we just looked at appears to be the document that is referred to as item number 13 in "sent and received dispatches" log-book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is written here that this is an addendum to the dispatch 01-18 of the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So even though this one is number 26, we've only got a total of 13 documents sent and received, according to the log-book. My question is: Is it possible that some communications were either not recorded in the log-book, as one possibility; another possibility is that they were sent by some other organisation than your communications centre and therefore not in the log-book. You allow for either of those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, the most likely explanation is that this addendum was sent. We described that log-book as the log-book of the communications centre at Vrace. Previously that's how we did it. And it's possible that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I think we agree on that, that it was sent. My question is -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you interrupted the witness when he tried to explain, explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I interrupted --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... give an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I interrupted because he was not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was. Believe me, he was. I don't know what you were getting through your ear -- your headphones, but he was explaining -- giving an explanation to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reading the transcript. The answer I was getting was: "According to me, the most likely explanation ... that this addendum was sent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, could you please ask the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we will hear his answer in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kezunovic. Maybe we had a miscommunication. I'm trying to understand how this document in item number 13, listed as 01-26 -- I had an inference that there were 25 earlier documents, and yet we only show 13 having been sent. And I was asking if you allowed for the possibility that one reason we only have 13 documents listed is that in the series 01-01 through 01-026 some of those documents may have been sent by other means than through your communications centre? Would you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are trying to get me to give you a yes or a no answer. Theoretically, yes. But there is an explanation that I can give you: I said earlier there were two communications centre of the MUP in its seat. One was located in Pale; one was located at Vrace. And it's possible that the previous document was sent from the Pale centre, whereas this one was sent the Vrace centre. And this is why there is this discrepancy in numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That makes sense to me. Because in this log-book, between the 22nd of April and the 13th of May, it appears that there were only a total of 49 dispatches sent and received. That seems like a low number, even given the fact that there were problems with communication links. It seems like a low number for MUP headquarters to be sending and receiving during that time-period. So if I understand you correctly, you're telling me we need to look and find a similar log-book for Pale for that time-period to get an idea of the total number of dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And regarding the question of communications sent by courier, I think you said last week that you personally didn't establish any kind of courier system within your communications centre. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It wasn't within my job description, within my administration. It didn't fall under our scope of duties, to organise the courier service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that couriers were used within the RS MUP in 1992 to deliver communications between some of the organisational units within the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be best if I were to illustrate it with an example. Whenever I went somewhere from Pale, I always asked whether I should take anything to anyone, whether somebody should come with me just to take advantage of the transportation I had. So the term "courier" does not include only an organised courier service; it also includes any member of the service travelling to another location. That person could also be deemed a courier, taking anything that needed to be taken, including mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was done in 1992 on occasion, wasn't it, that mail was delivered by courier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, by couriers. Equipment and written documents that I was supposed to send somewhere. I would, for example, say to my men, Is there somebody who's travelling on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday to such and such a location, and could that person take this with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time for the break, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, yesterday at page 11.637, in one of your answers to Mr. Zecevic, you talked about how sometimes in your communications centres you could send dispatches by circular. As I understood it, a circular was a means -- an electronic means where could you send a message to multiple recipients at the same time. For example, the CSB might be able to send the same dispatch to 15 SJBs at the same time, and that was called a circular. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. But it pertained to the period before the war. In the republic SUP, at its seat in the communications centre, there was a piece of equipment where all the lines ended, all the teleprinter system ended, from all centres for communication, from all municipalities. So by simply pushing a button, an operator would link up the seat of the MUP with another communications centre, and there were several types of circulars, MUP towards centre, MUP towards SJBs, MUP towards everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that during 1992, at least in CSB Banja Luka, there was still some capability to send circular to a partial number of the -- of the SJBs under Banja Luka because there was the equipment and the connections still in place? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in some stations. In some, perhaps. I would now have to go back and think about each station, how they were linked with Banja Luka, what lines existed, and then give you a separate individual answer for each station, and then add that all up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 11.640, on Friday, you were asked by Mr. Zecevic about the time when you had to go to Banja Luka to help establish the communications there. I think you were taking some of the -- some of the equipment and the documents for purposes of -- of sending coded communications. Is that correct? Is that why you went there personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. The greatest reason was to go there for the first time since the war started, to go there physically to the area, and to see what the situation was like on the ground, to talk to people, to see what problems they encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you a portion of something in Exhibit P573. This is the performance report for the period April to June 1992, dated 29 June, and it's regarding the work of the -- of the RS MUP. I'd like to show you something at page 8 of the English, and it's page 11 in the B/C/S. And this is the section of this report talking about duties and tasks related to communications and cryptographic protection. Yes, in that -- in that paragraph above item number 2, which is administrative and legal duties, I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think -- I need to go back one more page in the B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Here at the very bottom of the page, I think you're talking about some of the problems that existed because of the relocation of MUP headquarters to Pale, Vrace, Lukavica, and Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the top of the next page in B/C/S. I'm sorry, we're on the right page of English, but I needed to go to the next one of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kezunovic. And this report, dated 29th of June, 1992, says: "At this point, the Ministry of the Interior at its headquarters in Pale uses public telephone and telefax communications services [sic] to maintain contact with the Security Services Centres in Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Sarajevo, and short-wave systems for contact with the Trebinje and Sarajevo CSBs ..." You were shown by Mr. Zecevic today -- or Friday, and then it was referred to again today, about the report from -- from Doboj. If you didn't have a telefax or telephone communication with Doboj but only a short-wave contact, how were they to send in their daily reports? Do you know how that was done?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I don't -- I don't -- I hear what Mr. Hannis is reading, but the Serbian text does not correspond. I don't think that -- that the witness can see what -- what Mr. Hannis was reading to him. Maybe -- if am correct, this should be -- this should be page 12 of -- of Serbian text in the e-court. Maybe this can be shown to the witness so you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll defer to my learned friend. Can he indicate to me whether or not we're on the right page now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat which paragraph you wanted me to look at on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, if I can get some help from my learned friend across the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe you started reading from page 11, that's the previous page. Page 11 of the e-court in Serbian, the last paragraph. And then went on to -- to page 12, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, can you see the bottom of the page there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It should be page 11 of the e-court in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9. I can see the heading --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tasks concerning aliens, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the problem is the pages are numbered differently in the hard copy than they are in e-court, and I need to go -- yes, now I think we're on the correct page. And what I was reading from, Mr. Kezunovic, is the big paragraph above the number 2 at the bottom. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question was: If there was only a short-wave link with Trebinje and Sarajevo CSBs, how were communications made with them, in terms of sending coded dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read this paragraph to myself first so I see what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please state your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It appears that there were telefax and telephone communication links between headquarters in Pale with Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Sarajevo, but only short-wave links with Trebinje and Sarajevo. How were Trebinje and Sarajevo able to send in, for example, their daily reports that they were required to send? How was that done physically in 1992 prior to 29 June?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you read it, it says, in the third or fourth line from the top, that connections have been established via the public communications systems. Sarajevo is mentioned here also. And then an ultra short-wave link has been established with the Sarajevo CSB. This may be a -- an error in the text, but Sarajevo is mentioned twice, which -- and here it is stated that Sarajevo was connected both by short-wave radio and by public communications systems. Further down, it says: Short-wave link with the Sarajevo CSB -- or, rather, short-wave systems with contact with the Trebinje and Sarajevo CSBs. But this text is a bit confusing. Maybe the author wanted to show where telephone and telefax links existed and where just short-wave communications --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I understand, but my question is: Do you know, if indeed there were only short-wave links with Sarajevo and Trebinje CSB, how did they send in their daily reports prior to 29 June 1992? Did they use courier, did they send it by relay from some other station that he had a link with and ask them to forward it along some sort of relay? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, witness was interpreted -- interrupted when -- when he started to -- to give an explanation to the previous question. And it wasn't recorded at all. He was mention being something about analytics department. Maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm still trying to get an answer to the question. So either continue your previous answer or answer my repeated question, if you can. How would Trebinje and CSB Sarajevo get their daily reports to MUP headquarters in Pale, if there was only a short-wave link? Do you know? This is prior to 29 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is your question, how they transmitted their reports if they only had short-wave communication, then, well, short-wave communication must have been the way they transmitted their reports. But I suppose that at this time, in the month of June, they already had telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That relates to another question I was going to ask you. You remember last Friday we looked at the MUP annual report, and there was a reference to some 9.585 short-wave communications during the -- the reporting period for April through December 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, the intervention that Mr. Zecevic had made about an incomplete answer, we aren't sure whether that has been clarified, whether it is completely out of the way. Do we need to return to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm able to. What I propose to Your Honours is: When I'm done, if Mr. Zecevic feels it needs to be re-addressed, I don't oppose you allowing him one or two questions on re-cross to clear it up. But I think it would take me more time and effort than it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that would confuse matters. But if the witness could be assisted with whether he -- there was a portion of that earlier answer that he hadn't completed and that he would wish to give. You have the advantage of the transcript, Mr. Hannis. If you could take him back to the question and ask him directly whether there is a portion of his answer which he did not -- which we didn't get.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try to do it, Your Honour, but I think I have the disadvantage that the part that's missing is not in the transcript. And so I don't know if Mr. Zecevic can help me with me. I would ask if he can. Or Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, the simplest thing is to repeat your question. And your question was: "How were Trebinje and Sarajevo able to send in, for example, their daily report atlas they were required to send. How was that done physically in 1992, prior to the 29th of June?" And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness then continued in -- and answered that, referring to the document in front of him: "... if you read it, it says, in the third or fourth line from the top, that connections have been established via the public communications systems. Sarajevo is mentioned here also. And then an ultra short-wave link has been established with the Sarajevo CSB. This may be an error in the text, but Sarajevo is mentioned twice, which -- and here it is stated that Sarajevo was connected both by short-wave radio and by public communications systems. "Further down, it says: Short-wave link with the Sarajevo CSB -- or, rather, short-wave systems with contact with the Trebinje and Sarajevo CSBs. But this text is a bit confusing. Maybe the author wanted to show where telephone and telefax links existed and where just short-wave communications --" And this, Mr. Witness, is where you were cut off. Could you clarify the last part of your answer, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I wanted to say. That probably the purpose of this sentence was to say what there was, what was in existence by type of communication. And the centres mentioned first, Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Sarajevo, could be reached through public telephone and telefax communications; whereas, short-wave systems had to be used to contact Trebinje and Sarajevo. We were able to go to Trebinje physically through Montenegro. That was possible. We didn't, however, but that's another matter. Probably phone lines and telefax communications could be used at the beginning, so there was no need to insist on short-wave communication. But, you see, the question, as it was put to me, can be understood and answered only at a general level, not -- without going into the specifics; this or that existed or was established on such and such a date, et cetera. So I believe that I cannot give a yes or no answer. Something that I may have explained at great length on three to five pages, they wanted to put into one sentence, and then what you get is what you see here. I simply cannot make out what they wanted to say with this. I can only suppose that they wanted to say what -- the same that you concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And I certainly agree that you should not try and testify beyond your interpretation of -- of this letter. Mr. Witness, did you mention in your answer something about things being coordinated through an analytics department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned it to say that this summary report was made by the analyses and information department. We submit all our information to them, and they extract something from that in accordance with their methodology so as to give -- so as to present the essential things by organisational units. Before the war, these matters were not mentioned in any reports, if everything functioned all right. Communications are only mentioned when something is wrong. I was even criticised on several occasions that my maintenance staff were sitting idle. And I said, But that means that everything is working fine. But their answer was, No, no, you must give them something to work. And when communications are working impeccably, nobody commends us for it; but when something's wrong, then everybody complains that -- complains about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That seems to be a common experience in life. Thank you. I think this clarifies the matter. And, Mr. Hannis, I would ask you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, now I want to show you a document that's Exhibit P173. We looked at this before, but I think it relates to the subject at hand. And I need -- I will show you the first page. It's a communication from MUP headquarters, the minister. It's signed by someone else for him, it appears. It's dated the 16th of May to all the CSB chiefs. And I want to look particularly at something on page 3 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S. And in this section, the request is for reporting about war crimes. And for you it's the last paragraph above the stamp and the signature. And at the bottom of the page in English, it says: "In exceptional cases (breakdown of long-distance lines) you may send your reports to the following phone number ... which can you call ... if you have any questions or if something's not clear." First of all, do you recognise, by that phone number, where it would have been, geographically speaking?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 071 is the network prefix for Sarajevo. Probably this is a mistake, what we can see here in brackets. It probably shouldn't be long distance lines, but other lines. That is, breakdown of other lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But does is say in Serbian "long distance"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. But I think that's wrong. It should be "other" rather than "long-distance." So if other lines of communication are disrupted, then they should call this phone number, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the disruption of either long-distance lines or other lines was an exceptional circumstance; isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "in exceptional cases."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, you were asked about a document, I think, that was attempted to be sent from Prijedor at page 11.654.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have a look at Exhibit P668. Thank you. That's good for the English. If we could go to the next page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was a communication, and there was an indication handwritten on it that "we are not able to send this." It's addressed to MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the army of the Serbian Republic. Was the Prijedor SJB, would they have the communications, connections, or links to send something directly to the army? Was there that kind of communication link between SJBs and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because you cannot communicate with the army directly. In the army, it all has to go through the command and then down downward. That's why my conclusion would be that no direct link could have existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So this -- this message about "we're not able to send this" could refer to the addressee of the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two, which are underlined: The MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the SJBs physically able -- were any of the SJBs physically able to communicate directly to MUP headquarters in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never issued such an order. So if it isn't possible from our side, it isn't from the other either. But what does that mean any way, army of the Serbian Republic of BiH? It's the same as if I were to say, Send it to the people of Sarajevo or something. It's a much too general statement. It should have been much more specific, which unit, which body, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In -- in your previous answer, you said: I have never issued such an order. So if it's [sic] possible from our side, it's ... from the other either. I'm not sure your answer was correctly translated. Are you saying it was not possible from MUP headquarters to send a communication directly to an SJB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the SJBs. I was just saying that I never gave orders for SJBs to be able to link up with the military units, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about police and military. I'm just talking about within the MUP. Was the Ministry of Interior, in headquarters, could the minister send a communication directly to an SJB? For example, in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it was technically possible. I would have to know whether, on that date, it was physically possible for -- for him to send out a communication. And what do I mean by technical possibilities? If it's a coded dispatch, they must have encoders and decoders and codes-books and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But how about an open communication, uncoded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, if, on that date, whichever date you're talking about, it was possible to send something to Bijeljina, then it was possible to send it to Zvornik too because both belonged to the same network area. They have the same network prefix. If you dial 06 to call some number in Bijeljina -- sorry. 076. Then you could also reach a number connected to the exchange in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You agreed with Mr. Zecevic on Friday, at page 11.661, when he asked you about the communications centre of the Ministry of Defence facing identical problems because it was linked up with the PTT system. And he went on further, and you agreed with him, when he said: "... they," I guess meaning the Ministry of Defence, "needed at least three months, or rather, over three months to establish any kind of communication at all from that centre?" And you said: "Yes, that's right." What was your source of information about the Ministry of Defence's communications centre and whatever difficulties they may have had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My source were the people working there, that is, from the assistant minister Colonel Kotlica, through Major Regopagic [phoen], through to the office -- the other officers working there. Kotlica called me once from Pale to come and see them and to talk to them. And on that occasion, he spoke to me about their problems. He had to integrate all the municipalities, that is, the municipal Assemblies, the civilian structures, and all the various services which was much more demanding than the problem that I had with the police. Because they didn't have communications centres in the municipalities. They used to, in peacetime; but in war time, it was an open question what had remained in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately when you had that conversation with Colonel Kotlica, what month?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been late April or early May, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I started to ask you this before. In the MUP annual report, there's a reference to short-wave communications. This is Exhibit P625. And I don't know if you'll remember the number, but it's at page 30 -- I'm sorry, page 27 of the English, and I believe in e-court it's page 37 and going on over to page 38. In Friday's transcript at page 11.671, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about this and pointed out that this seemed to be an extremely high number. Actually, I think for the substance of this part of the sentence -- we see the last three words on this page, Mr. -- the last three or four words on this page, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could show him the next page in B/C/S regarding the 9.585.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic said: You gave us an explanation then that this number was extremely high ... but you also explained that these were only tests of connections, that there was no actual traffic using that backup system." My question is: Are you saying this number of 9.585 short-wave radio connections mentioned in the annual report, those are all nothing but sound checks - someone calling up and saying, Can you hear me; yes, I can hear you - and nothing else? Is that what all 9.585 were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly it was that way. Whether somebody sent a short dispatch -- well, what I explained, the difference between sending coded dispatches by teleprinter, that is, machine processed, as compared to manual processing or coding of dispatches, which is very slow. And we would have gotten nowhere. But this backup system was meant to enable us to send out dispatches if everything else fails, to send them out and receive them. And perhaps somebody had time enough and decided, Okay, we'll send out this dispatch through short-wave communication. But because there was no -- there were no explicit orders that they should or should not do that. So perhaps they had lots of time and wanted to test this type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But if I understood you correctly when we looked at the MUP performance report for the months April through June 1992, you remember we discussed that and it showed that there were public telephone and telefax communications with Banja Luka, Doboj, and Bijeljina; but for Trebinje and CSB Sarajevo, there were short-wave links. And, if I understood your answer earlier to that, you said that they must have sent their daily reports by short wave because they didn't have a telephone or telefax communication as of 29 June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- but let's me add something and then I'll answer your question. In one of the documents, you could see telephone numbers. And you saw that next to Trebinje there was a 089, which is a Montenegrin number. I don't know from which switchboard. In any case, telecom provided for the functioning of the public system via Montenegro. Nobody could ban that or any such thing, which means that somebody from the centre took a number. And now can I answer your question. I can provide a complete answer. Maybe a number of dispatches were sent by KT, but most of them were sent via this telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last question on -- 9.585, it -- it seems unusual to me that in an annual report for the working of the MUP in a section about the communications and cryptographic data protection administration that you would mention 9.585 sound checks. Do you understand my question? That's -- that seems kind of silly. Who cares that you called up 9.000 times to see if the sound was working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to answer in the following way: You're absolutely right. Your question is very justified. Believe me, it doesn't make sense to me either. But what's on paper is highly in disputable. I never checked; I never did the maths; somebody else did the maths. This may be a mistake. Maybe it's 958, not 9585. It might be 958, which would have made much more sense. Maybe there was a centre which could carry out more checks, but that was up to them. In any case, what you see on paper are the facts. And what I'm telling you are just my views. You're absolutely right. Why would anybody in their right mind make so many checks? Still, there have to be checks. For example, if you have reserve vehicles parked somewhere for a long time, you still need to check whether they are in a good state of repair. Before the war we had a situation - have you to believe me when I tell you - when it was -- that it was totally unexpected for all of us when we checked the status of some vehicles that were on stand by, it turned out that only one of them could actually be started. And even that vehicle had a problem, either the tank was empty or something. So from then on, everything had to be checked weekly. There was an order for weekly checks of all the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your answer. I'm asking if you would entertain the possibility that that number, 9.585, not only includes sound checks but also includes substantive short-wave communications where information was exchanged. Perhaps somebody sending in their daily report from Trebinje, for example.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
