utterances.text: In theory, yes. Why do I say "in theory"? Because everything that was done had to be recorded. There had to be a paper trail after everything. Which means that somebody handed over ten; those ten had to be recorded in the short-wave log. There's no dilemma about that. And now that you are asking me and you want a general answer, I can tell you that, in principle, yes, that was the case. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understood the way the annual report was prepared was that, for example, for your administration, the communications administration, you prepared a report that went to the analytical guys who wrote up this overall report and that before it became final, all you administrative heads got together in a meeting with the analytical guys and went over the report. So you had a chance to make any corrections or additions that you thought were necessary. That's right, isn't it? Isn't that what you told me last week?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't gather all of us together. There were people who were tasked with writing a paper. That person would make rounds of all the units and discuss the matter. If somebody had asked me, for example, when it comes to the short-wave links, I would have never recorded them. But they thought that that was an important data, and I didn't have any reason to oppose them. If they thought it was important, why not? In my view, it wasn't. And I'm sure that I voiced that opinion with the person, if they asked me about my opinion. I'm sure that I told them that there are much more important things that weren't even mentioned in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You strike me as a person who might also voice your opinion about something like that even if you weren't asked, because you were a professional in communications. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I am -- even now, I am telling you everything. I'm answering your questions, but I'm also telling you things that you don't ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Next I want to ask you about a few things that came up today. At page 7, line 6, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about in early 1993 you don't have communications with about 30 per cent of the organisational units. You remember that he showed you the part of the report that talked about 70 per cent were conducted. And -- and most of that, it appears, was done recently. Isn't it correct that during 1992, from April 1992 on, that there were certain portions of the territory in the former Bosnia that were captured or liberated, depending on your term of choice, that had previously been held by the Bosnian Muslims and/or the Bosnian Croats, and it was necessary, then, to establish new connections with this newly conquered or captured territorial where there was now a new SJB for the RS MUP. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. Let me just give you one example: At the time, Mostar was called Serbian Mostar. Actually it was a village Zimlje [phoen]. And if I gave you all topographic maps, a guide, a car, I'm not even sure that he would be able to locate it in the course of one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to ask you about this topic that Mr. Zecevic covered with you regarding the number of dispatches pre-war. First of all, pre-war, do you know how many SJBs were there in Bosnia, in all of Bosnia, in early 1992 or late 1991? Do you know that number?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. 109. Ten centres and 109 SJBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in -- in April or May of 1992, after the -- after the war started, I understand there were five centres in the RS MUP. Do you know how many SJBs there were in May, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some reservation, I counted them, and that number oscillated. We didn't know for sure. But it may have been even 60, plus/minus a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that question, he said you mentioned an approximate number of 300.000 received and sent dispatches from the communications centre of the MUP headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the MUP headquarters, in the Republican SUP. I remember I -- I remember the data about coding. There were about 120.000 coded dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to be clear. Is that sent and received in the headquarters of the MUP, or is that number for all the organisational units of the MUP? It seems like an extremely high number.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a high number. And that's what was sent and what was received by the MUP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During what time-period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Going back how many years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1990s, let's say. Or in the late 1980s or early 1990s. You see, when I started working in the Republican SUP, not even 50 per cent of the bodies had their codes, and I mean municipal secretariats. The development of the system is of a recent date, and the development followed a project system that provided for the complete overhaul so nothing had to be added to the system. Everybody could contact everybody else. They could send the dispatches but coded and uncoded to everybody else. And we had physical capacity, according to the then-technology of the coding of dispatches that Mr. Zecevic mentioned, according to which the dispatch was brought to somebody, it was coded on teleprinter or, rather, sent by teleprinter, coded, and so on and so forth. Following a procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me try and understand this. That number, 300.000, is it for a period of one year, three years, ten years? What time-period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. From January 1991 to December 31st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, in the late 1980s or the earlier 1990s, as of 1991, I was no longer privy to the system. I've already described my position. I did that in answering Mr. Zecevic's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. By my rough math, if that's for a one-year period, 300.000 works out to something like 820 a day. That's like one dispatch sent and/or received every two minutes or less than every two minutes for a 24-hour period. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can do your maths in very general terms. However, that's how things were. I don't know how long the dispatches were. But we had five teleprinters and all people did were -- there was typing 24/7, five people typed dispatches. They were three other men who were in charge of coding. Seven or eight were working in the communications centre of the MUP. There was a procedure. And before the war, we had a short-wave network that also functioned and had a machine code through which a number of dispatches were sent in order to double-check the functioning of the system. But, having said that, I also have to tell you that at that time we had more staff and we could entertain a bigger workload.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where does that 300.000 number come from? Is that just a number you have in your head, or is it that in a report somewhere that I could find and look at?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports. And in those reports, there was a separate report for the department in charge of the data transfer or, rather, this sending of dispatches, both coded and uncoded. They had to record the quantity of materials that -- that was used, the codes used, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic asked you, and you agreed with him in his assumption, that in war time it would be logical to expect a rise in the number of dispatches by at least 30 per cent. And you said, Yes, you're right, at least 30 per cent. What do you base that number on? I mean, before 1992, you never had the experience of the MUP being in a war in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how -- how did you estimate that, Oh, the war started, dispatches are going to go up by 30 per cent? Why did you think that? It just seemed like a guess.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was this: Would the quantity of dispatches go up by at least 30 per cent? And that word "by at least;" that's the key. Not 30 per cent, but "at least," a minimum. And it was my logic, if the activities were the same, if the state of crime was the same, if the traffic control was the same, wouldn't it be logical that new events emerged during war time that would increase that quantity of events by at least one third? That was the logic that I followed in my answer. I don't know whether that was the whole logic followed in the question that was put to me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this way: During peacetime, before the war, when there were 300.000 dispatches sent and received, it seems to me a lot of those dispatches during peacetime would have been about things that were not important during war time. I mean, didn't you have dispatches about Ahmed Ahmic or Mile Milic is appointed to a certain position in Zvornik SJB or some minor police station? All kinds of administrative and logistical and technical kind of things that weren't crucial in the war time situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So to me, as a civilian and not having gone through that experience, it seems like you might just as well expect the number of dispatches to go down by more than 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about one's impressions or your impressions as a layperson, as a civilian, who is not savvy in the work of the police, but from the point of view of somebody who lived with the police, I know how the police think. And the only way things could go was up. Because in war time, people would even send dispatches to ask the time because they did not coordinate their times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any examples in -- in 1992 of people sending a dispatch to ask the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a watch; I didn't have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kezunovic, I don't have any further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish a safe journey back to your home. Thank you. The usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where are we in relation to your following witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. One is in relation to the next witness. It's my understanding the Prosecution is requesting that we not begin her testimony until tomorrow morning because of her arrival time and the proofing that's been going on. I understand the Defence doesn't have an objection to that request, if it's agreeable with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Was this the matter in respect of which you had asked for the five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's one. I have a second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear your second issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second one, Your Honour, relates to your oral decision or indication Friday at the end of the day concerning the Prosecution's pending motion to add witnesses. And we -- we'll certainly be able to provide the list of summaries for those witnesses we want to add and have asked for a report on the state of disclosure. I can give you a preliminary report on the state of disclosure and then make a request. It's my understanding that the correct number of witnesses we're talking about is 53. I think it said 57 somewhere, but I've learned that I think we have four names duplicated. So the correct number, I believe, is 53. It's my understanding that we're up to date on disclosure regarding 22 of those witnesses that we've disclosed statements and prior testimonies for. There are an additional four for whom we have made partial disclosure already. This is at least a statement for four of those witnesses. Another eight are common witnesses with the Karadzic case, and that should be easy to make the disclosure because cut and paste. That leaves 19 that we haven't made any disclosure yet. We would like to request Your Honours consider the possibility of delaying the disclosure on those 19 witnesses until perhaps you have made an indication about whether any of them may be called by the Prosecution. My reasoning is this: If these witnesses aren't going to be called, then we will have made disclosure, including some personal information, et cetera, that will be out there, and they're not coming as witnesses. We think that there will be sufficient information in the motion and the summary for you to make an informed decision about whether or not it might be appropriate for the Prosecution to call this witness. If you decide no, well, then no disclosure has been made, and that witness has no privacy concerns about things that have been disclosed relating to them. If you decide, Yes, we are going to call that witness, then we will make full disclosure for those remaining 19 witnesses. And if the Defence has an issue at that time saying, This is 10.000 pages; I need more time to prepare for these 19 witnesses, we can address it at that time. That's my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And so we appreciated that the matter of disclosure would be a running exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And there are some protective measures, motions, for the Trial Chamber to deal with that may pertain to some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just two comments. We were very explicit about the fact that we cannot give a proper response to the motion unless we receive the disclosure. And it's -- I am quite astonished that my learned friend uses the word "out there." It's not out there; it is given to the Defence. And the Defence has the obligations as it has. So the information is not out there; it is given to us with all the limits that we have to disclose this information to anybody else, and we need this information to be able to respond to the motion. It's a very simple situation, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You were -- and I thought Mr. Krgovic was about to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When it comes to the disclosure, the issue is that some of the statements and parts thereof were disclosed at different times, in different forms, and now we have to connect all those materials and identify them. We would kindly ask the Prosecutor to put all those materials together and disclose them all at once. That would save us a lot of time because some things may have been disclosed recently. Some may have been disclosed six months ago. All of which is demanding on the Defence resources and time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in my comment at the end of Mr. Hannis's statement, I used the word -- I used the phrase "running exercise" as a way of explaining that contrary to Mr. Krgovic's desire that this happens all at once, that the Trial Chamber appreciates the practical difficulties or practical considerations which the Prosecution has to bear in mind. However, notwithstanding that, as Mr. Zecevic has, in my view, correctly put his finger on the -- on the resolution, that is, that it is simple in the sense that the Prosecution would appreciate that whatever choices they make, there are consequences that flow from it. And they would - we assume - prudently conduct themselves accordingly. So the requirement that the Defence is not embarrassed or caught by surprise is something that the Chamber is very alive to. And it is part of the Chamber's duty to safe-guard the interests of the Defence in this regard. So if there is nothing further that need delay us, we would take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
